## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 3/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
Follow-up research pass for the same project as before (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me, an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites). A prior deep-research pass covered six areas but only areas 1 (data/info visualization) and 2 (component patterns) survived adversarial verification — 12 and 2 confirmed claims respectively. Areas 3, 4, 5 and 6 produced ZERO surviving claims, because the verification pass demanded peer-reviewed or normative-spec sources, and this material largely does not live there. This pass covers ONLY those four areas, with an explicitly adjusted source policy.

SOURCE POLICY FOR THIS PASS — two tiers, both admissible, but every surviving claim must be tagged with its tier:
- TIER A (normative/measured): W3C/WHATWG specs, platform HIG (Apple, Material, Microsoft Fluent), peer-reviewed HCI research, MDN, official framework docs (View Transitions API, CSS spec text).
- TIER B (practitioner/consensus, admissible but flagged): named practitioners with a track record (e.g. Josh Comeau, Emil Kowalski, Rauno Freiberg, Jhey Tompkins, Sarah Drasner, Val Head, Jakob Nielsen's NN/g, Awwwards/CSS Design Awards jury commentary, newsroom graphics desk blog posts, conference talks with slides/video), and cross-source consensus (the same specific claim independently stated by 2+ unaffiliated named practitioners counts as corroboration even with no peer-reviewed backing). Do NOT admit anonymous SEO listicles, content-mill blogs, or AI-generated roundups — a claim needs an identifiable, credentialed author or organization behind it either way. When verifying a Tier B claim, the adversarial verifier's job is to check whether the source actually says what's claimed and whether it's presented as consensus or as one person's opinion — not to demand it be peer-reviewed research, since it structurally isn't.

THE FOUR AREAS:

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS AND THE ANTI-GENERIC DISCOURSE — named aesthetic/interaction movements in web and product design current as of 2025-2026 (e.g. things like brutalist-minimalism, kinetic typography revival, AI-native/glassy gradients, retro-futurism, anti-design, whatever is actually current — do not assume the answer, find it). For each: its defining mechanics, its characteristic failure mode, the condition under which it's the right choice. ALSO, separately and just as important: what now specifically reads as generic, templated, or "AI-default" in 2025-2026 web design — the tells that mark a site as templated (specific patterns, not vague complaints) — and the named discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design (design critics, studios, or practitioners who have written specifically about this). This section feeds a real open question about whether documenting current movements at all serves or undermines an anti-template mandate — surface any source that speaks to that tension.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION IMPLEMENTATION — the View Transitions API (both same-document and cross-document): what it actually does, its current browser support reality, its documented failure modes and gotchas from practitioners who've shipped with it. Shared-element/container transforms (FLIP technique and its named descendants). Disclosure and expansion motion patterns (accordion, drawer, sheet open/close motion specifically — not just their accessibility contract, which is already covered). Chart entrance/transition/morphing animation. Staggering and orchestration patterns (named techniques, not generic "stagger the children"). Scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals, including the native CSS `animation-timeline`/`scroll()`/`view()` functions versus JS scroll libraries, with real support/performance tradeoffs. Spring/physics-based motion versus duration-and-easing curves: is there real guidance (platform HIG counts as Tier A here) on when each is correct, not just "springs feel nice"?

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the actual anatomy/principles framework for a micro-interaction (trigger, rules, feedback, loop/mode — this is a named framework by Dan Saffer, verify it precisely rather than assuming). Feedback and affordance signalling for hover/focus/press/drag states specifically. Optimistic UI as a pattern: what it is, when it's right, its failure mode when the optimistic action fails. Haptics and sound as feedback channels for web (not native apps) — is there real guidance or is this mostly unaddressed for web. TIMING NUMBERS SPECIFICALLY: what duration/easing ranges are attributed to actual platform guidance (Material Design's motion duration tokens, Apple HIG's timing guidance) versus what is repeated folklore with no real source (e.g. the ubiquitous "100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the limit before attention wanders" chain — trace this to Jakob Nielsen's actual 1993 "Response Times: The 3 Important Limits" if that's really the source, and report exactly what it says versus what's commonly misquoted).

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress bars: is there real evidence (Tier A or strong Tier B) for skeleton screens improving perceived performance over spinners, or is this also folklore? Look specifically for any controlled study, not just practitioner assertion. Streaming/progressive rendering as a perceived-performance technique. Optimistic and predictive loading patterns. Designed preloaders as a deliberate choice (this repo's own doctrine already treats a preloader as a first-class design deliverable, not a spinner — look for what actually justifies that position). Cumulative Layout Shift avoidance techniques — this one IS well-specified (it's a Core Web Vitals metric with a Google-published measurement methodology), so it should be strong Tier A.

DELIVERABLE — same shape as before: landscape per area with concrete named patterns/movements, mechanics, documented failure mode, the condition under which each is right, and citations tagged Tier A or Tier B. Explicitly separate "verified consensus" from "single-source opinion" from "unverifiable folklore" — the folklore-detection is as valuable an output as the confirmed claims, especially for the timing numbers in area 5, since that repo has a HARD rule (§5) that no unsourced claim ships. End with the same kind of repo-mapping section as before: what belongs in STYLES.md (four-part shape: mechanics/Implies/Fails/Right when), what belongs in CRAFT.md (Technique/What it is/Where it earns its place), what's new material, and explicitly answer the open question about whether documenting current style movements helps or hurts an anti-template pipeline.

## Claim under review
"The API's transition mechanism works via a pseudo-element tree that captures a static snapshot of the pre-transition state and a live version of the post-transition state, which is the technical basis for its shared-element/FLIP-style morphing effect."

**Source:** https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "::view-transition-old() — A static snapshot of the old view, before the transition. ::view-transition-new() — A live representation of the new view, after the transition."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

# View Transition API: Pseudo-elements and Snapshots

Based on the provided MDN content, here are the relevant pseudo-elements:

## Pseudo-elements Definition

The content describes the following pseudo-elements:

**`::view-transition-old()`**
> "A static snapshot of the old view, before the transition."

**`::view-transition-new()`**
> "A live representation of the new view, after the transition."

**`::view-transition-image-pair()`**
> "The container for a view transition's old and new views — before and after the transition."

**`::view-transition-group()`**
> "The root of a single view transition."

**`::view-transition`**
> "The root of the view transitions overlay, which contains all view transitions and sits over the top of all other page content."

## Snapshot Concept

The content mentions snapshots in context of the `view-transition-scope` property:

> "`view-transition-scope`: Enables the discoverability of elements with `view-transition-name` values set on them (and therefore the creation of view transition **snapshots**) to be isolated to a specific element subtree."

## Shared Element/Morphing Transitions

The provided content does **not include specific text describing shared element or morphing transitions**. However, it does reference:

- **`view-transition-name`** property: "Specifies the view transition snapshot that selected elements will participate in, which enables an element to be animated separately from the rest of the page during a view transition."

This indicates the API supports animating individual elements, which is related to morphing/shared element concepts, but detailed documentation of this feature is referenced in the separate guide: "[Using element-scoped view transitions](/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API/Using_element-scoped)."

content.content:
# View Transitions: FLIP vs. Shared-Element Approach

This page does **not** explicitly describe the View Transition mechanism using FLIP terminology. Instead, it explains the technique through **pseudo-element architecture** that achieves shared-element transition effects.

## How the Pseudo-Elements Work Together

The documentation describes the structural hierarchy:

> "::view-transition ├─ ::view-transition-group(root) │ └─ ::view-transition-image-pair(root) │ ├─ ::view-transition-old(root) │ └─ ::view-transition-new(root)"

The mechanism relies on **automatic position/size morphing**. As stated:

> "The `::view-transition-group` also transitions: Position and transform (using a `transform`), Width, Height"

The old view (a screenshot) and new view (live representation) are both positioned identically within their group container. The group itself animates dimensional changes between states, while opacity crossfades the content layers.

## Why This Differs from FLIP

Rather than explicitly capturing, playing, and inverting positions like FLIP does, View Transitions automates this by:

1. Capturing element snapshots before DOM updates
2. Creating a pseudo-element tree that handles the morphing automatically
3. Letting CSS animations drive the visual transition

The approach is more declarative than FLIP—developers assign `view-transition-name` properties and let the browser handle the coordinate transformation calculations.

# View Transition Pseudo Tree Overview

## Structure Description

The article explains that the view transition pseudo tree consists of hierarchical pseudo-elements triggered when a view transition is initiated. The structure includes:

- `::view-transition` (root container)
- `::view-transition-group` (handles position, size, rotation animation)
- `::view-transition-image-pair` (applies isolation)
- `::view-transition-old` and `::view-transition-new` (represent start/end states)

## Key Technical Details

The article describes how the browser automatically captures element states: *"Each pseudo-element plays a distinct role in how the view transition animates. The browser does most of the heavy lifting."*

It notes that `::view-transition-old` and `::view-transition-new` *"represent what the element looks like at the start and end of the animation."*

## Gaps in Comparison

**The article does not mention the FLIP technique or establish connections to shared-element transitions.** It also doesn't discuss whether the pseudo tree represents static snapshots versus live DOM representations, nor does it explain morphing effects. The focus remains on the technical structure and default browser behaviors rather than comparative animation methodologies.

I found several relevant results about the View Transitions API and its connection to the FLIP technique and Jake Archibald's work. Here's what the search revealed:

## View Transitions API and FLIP

The View Transition API can handle transitions more naturally by just updating the DOM and letting the browser animate the shared element, as opposed to the manual FLIP technique. The FLIP technique is a pattern where you manually measure elements to create animations.

## Jake Archibald's Role

Jake Archibald is one of the developers behind the View Transition API. He has been trying to convince Chrome to implement the feature for years, and they are now doing so. Jake Archibald's excellent View Transitions article covers the details well.

## Shared Element Transitions

During a transition, the browser finds an element named in the old state and an element with the same name in the new state (even if they're completely different elements in different parts of the page) and animates between their two positions and sizes. This eliminates the need for manual FLIP animations in many cases.

## FLIP as a Fallback

Some implementations use a same-document FLIP fallback that keeps elements moving regardless of browser support, with the fallback measuring from/to rectangles and faking the morph via transform: translate + scale.
